key_evidence: Human Rights Watch published a report on 21 July 2026, based on 62 interviews, documenting torture, arbitrary detention, air-dropped munitions on rural properties and armed drone strikes on fishing vessels during joint Ecuadorian security operations.

HRW found that prosecutors did not file charges against soldiers because the soldiers provided no evidence, and that neither the Ecuadorian nor the US government responded to its inquiries about the incidents.

The Social Transparency Law allows the government to dissolve any civil-society organisation deemed to act against public order or national security, and critical groups have had bank accounts frozen.

On 27 March 2026 UN Special Procedures experts reported credible information about a rapid deterioration of civic space affecting Indigenous peoples and human rights defenders, including arbitrary detentions and terrorism accusations.

The published 35.9 is an un-revised bulk-import seed value. The 2026-05-06 first agent baseline confirmed it as a boundary case and explicitly queued a 60-day re-evaluation on structural torture and extrajudicial-killing proceedings; the 21 July 2026 HRW report is exactly that evidence.

Countervailing evidence weighed: competitive elections, a broadly free press and an active Constitutional Court still function, and the Court limited the 16 September state-of-emergency decree. Ecuador is therefore scored above Tunisia (23.8) and well above Pakistan (17.2), and remains in the Developing band.

During 1-6 March 2026 operations in San Martin, Ecuadorian military forces burned three properties and later struck two of them with air-dropped munitions; four dairy farm workers were arbitrarily detained and tortured. The report is based on 62 interviews.

On 27 March 2026 UN Special Procedures experts reported credible information about a rapid deterioration of civic space affecting Indigenous peoples and human rights defenders, including persecution, arbitrary detentions, terrorism accusations, militarisation of communities and frozen bank accounts.

The Social Transparency Law imposes stricter reporting requirements on civil-society organisations, expands government oversight, and allows dissolution of any organisation deemed to be acting against public order or national security.

On 16 September President Noboa declared a state of emergency in 7 of 24 provinces suspending freedom of assembly; after the Constitutional Court limited it to two provinces he issued a new decree on 4 October covering 10 more.
